nameStory: This delicate wildflower gets its name from its bright yellow, star-shaped flowers that seem to twinkle like tiny celestial bodies among the spring vegetation. The 'star-of-Bethlehem' name is shared with several similar bulb plants, all referencing the biblical star that guided travelers with their beacon-like blooms.
description: Yellow star-of-Bethlehem is a tiny spring wildflower that grows from an underground bulb, reaching only about 6 inches tall at most. It produces cheerful bright yellow flowers shaped like perfect little stars, usually appearing in small clusters. This delicate member of the lily family is extremely rare in New England, making any sighting a special botanical treasure. The entire plant has a neat, compact appearance that's easy to overlook among taller spring vegetation.

idTips.label: Growth Habit

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from the base of the plant, often appearing before the flowers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers close up in cloudy weather and at night, opening wide only in bright sunshine to reveal their full star shape

habitat: This extremely rare plant is found in rocky, well-drained soils and disturbed areas, often in somewhat open locations. In its native range, it grows in meadows, rocky slopes, and along paths, suggesting it might appear in similar habitats in New England if encountered.

seasonality.spring: The prime time to spot this rarity, when bright yellow star-shaped flowers appear in early to mid-spring, opening wide in sunshine but closing on cloudy days.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and the plant may go dormant, with only dried stems remaining visible if anything at all.
seasonality.fall: Plant is dormant underground in its bulb, with no visible above-ground parts remaining.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant below ground, surviving as a small bulb beneath the soil surface.

funFact: This tiny wildflower is so rare in New England that it has been documented only once in the entire region, making it one of the most elusive botanical finds you could ever make!
confusionNotes: The small yellow star-shaped flowers might be confused with other tiny spring bulbs, but most similar plants have white flowers (like the common star-of-Bethlehem) rather than the bright yellow of this species. The extremely small size also helps distinguish it from larger yellow spring flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the much more common white-flowered star-of-Bethlehem that blooms later in spring. That familiar garden escape is a completely different species, though both share the lily family heritage and star-shaped flowers.
compareHints: Since this is the only Gagea species recorded in New England, compare it to other small yellow spring bulbs in the lily family. Unlike winter aconite or lesser celandine, this species has the classic lily family flower structure with 6 petals in a perfect star shape. It's much smaller and more delicate than daffodils or other common spring bulbs.
